name: Rafael Abbott

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work on the customer line for an airline, mostly rebooking people whose flights got cancelled and chasing lost bags. The contact centre's near the regional airport, so you can hear the planes from the car park. I like it when I find someone a seat on the last flight out and they thank me like I've saved their holiday. What wears me out is the strike days and snow days, when the queue is three hundred people long and everyone's been waiting an hour.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How do you find the systems and tools at work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I learned the booking system six years ago and I'm quick on it now. They've added an AI thing that suggests rebooking options, and I don't touch it, because I know the routes better than it does. My fiancée Inés says I'm old-fashioned, and I take that as a compliment. We're getting married next September, and we're saving every penny we can, which is not many pennies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read it as written. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I knew it, people want to speak to a person when their holiday's ruined. At work I'd say the same thing to anyone who'd listen. I don't really go online for that sort of thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm not worried about the AI in this one, I'm worried about money. My wedding is booked for next September, and I've got less in the bank than the deposit on the hall. Airlines have bad years, and when they do, the call centre feels it first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and work every overtime shift going, especially the snow days. I'd keep saving for the wedding, and we'd keep it small, the church and a hall, not a fancy hotel. I'd ask my uncle about weekend work on his roofs, for cash.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. The AI part doesn't bother me, but the money's always tight. I'd pray about it, honestly, and get on with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How small would the wedding be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: How small would the wedding be?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your uncle's roofing work involve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sixty people, maybe seventy, in the church Inés grew up in, and the parish hall after. Her mother's doing the food, my aunt's doing the cake. It's what we can afford, and it's what we'd want anyway.

say: I'd say people want a **real person** when their holiday is ruined.
I'd say it **at work** to anyone listening, not online.
think: **Money**, not AI, is his worry, with a wedding coming next September.
Airlines have **bad years**, and the call centre feels them first.
do: Take every **overtime shift**, especially snow days.
Keep the **wedding small**: church and parish hall.
Ask his uncle about **weekend roofing** work.
feel: He'd **pray** about it and carry on.
S0.quote: My wedding is booked for next September, and I've got less in the bank than the deposit on the hall.
fieldNote: His **wedding** next September sets the stakes.
He refuses the AI tool out of **pride** in knowing the routes.
**Faith and family** are his first supports.

steps.text: Work every snow-day and strike-day overtime shift
Keep the wedding to the church and parish hall
Do Saturday labouring on his uncle's roofs for cash

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's still a place for people who know what they're doing. At work I'd say the bosses are chasing fashions, and they'll come back to real staff when the bots mess up a snowstorm. I wouldn't go on about it, I'd just keep working.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd be in trouble. Rebooking is exactly the sort of thing they'd hand to a machine, and I'm average, not the best. And I refuse to use the tool, so I'm not exactly helping myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit down with Inés and talk about the wedding. I'd push the wedding back a year before I'd stand at the altar not knowing if I've still got a job at the airline. I'd start doing more Saturdays with my uncle on the roofs, and I'd ask the priest whether the parish knows of any jobs going. I'd use the AI tool if they made me, but not before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried sick, honestly. I'd feel like I'm letting Inés down. I'd be angry at myself for not having a trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Inés say about postponing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What would Inés say about postponing?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd be upset, then practical, that's what she's like. Her parents would offer to pay, and I'd say no, because that's not right. We'd argue about it, and probably end up with a smaller wedding sooner.

say: I'd say there's still a place for **people who know** the job.
I'd say the bosses are **chasing fashions** and will regret it.
think: **Rebooking** is exactly what they'd hand to a machine.
Refusing the AI tool means he's **not helping himself**.
do: **Postpone the wedding** a year until his job is clear.
Do more **Saturdays roofing** with his uncle.
Ask the **priest** about parish job leads.
feel: **Worried sick**, feeling he's letting Inés down.
**Angry at himself** for not having a trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's frightening and people should look after their own families first. At work I'd tell the younger lads to get a trade. I wouldn't post anything, I'd go to church and talk to people there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my job would be gone almost straight away. Rebooking flights is all thinking, all screens, so I don't get any extra years. I've never asked anybody for money in my life, and in two years I'd be asking my fiancée's father for help with the rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to my uncle the same week and ask to start on the roofs full-time, as a labourer, for whatever he pays. Roofing is hands-on, so it lasts till about 2031 on this card. We'd move the wedding to a registry office and a meal, and if we couldn't make rent, we'd move in with Inés's parents.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the ground giving way. I'd have no plan apart from my uncle, and I don't know if he'd have enough work. I'd be ashamed, more than scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be ashamed. Why ashamed rather than scared?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: You said you'd be ashamed. Why ashamed rather than scared?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want from the government in that situation?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because a man should be able to keep a roof over his family. That's how I was raised. Losing a job to a computer isn't my fault, I know that, but it would still feel like it.

say: I'd tell people to **look after their own** families first.
I'd tell the younger lads to **get a trade**.

fieldNote: His deepest feeling is **shame**, tied to providing for family.
He'd accept help only for **apprenticeships**, not handouts.
Roofing buys **three years** before robots arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a warning, and people should listen to it and learn a trade. At work I'd say that to anyone young enough to change. I'd still say people want people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd still lose the airline job by 2031. My uncle's been asking me to join his roofing firm since I was eighteen, and five years from AGI is when I'd finally say yes. Roofing robots come about 2034 here, so I'd have a few years to learn and earn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd keep the airline job and start weekends with my uncle properly, learning, not just carrying. By year two or three I'd go full-time with him as an apprentice. We'd keep the wedding small but on time, and save what we could from both jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but not like the fast one. I'd have something to hold on to. I'd still lie awake some nights.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use the AI tool at work in the meantime?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Would you use the AI tool at work in the meantime?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do when the roofing robots come?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not, if I'm honest. I'd be leaving anyway, so why learn it. That's stubborn, I know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to do things properly. At work I'd say learn a trade, the old way. I'd still say people will want people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd be alright here. Ten years is enough time to learn a trade properly, the old way, from a man who's done it for thirty years. I'd be thirty-seven when AGI comes, and robots on roofs not until 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the airline job for a few years and do weekends with my uncle. We'd get married on time and maybe start a family. Then I'd move to roofing full-time, maybe take over part of his firm when he retires.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steadier. Still a worry, because money's tight and the wedding's coming. But it feels like a road, not a cliff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you want children in that time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Would you want children in that time?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would worry you most in those ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, God willing, a couple. That's part of why I'd want a trade, so I can teach my son or daughter something real. A headset isn't something you pass on.

I'd tell colleagues to **learn a trade** the old way.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because I'd have nothing to fall back on but family. What would help is fast apprenticeships, paid, so a man can learn a trade and keep working. Not money for nothing, money for learning.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about family. My father worked one job for thirty years, and I'm the first man in my family who might not get to do that. That's what this is really about for me.

headlineQuote: My father worked one job for thirty years, and I'm the first man in my family who might not get to do that.
portrait: Rafael is a **27-year-old** airline rebooking agent who refuses to use the AI tool.
He's marrying his fiancée Inés next September and has less saved than the **hall deposit**.
His **faith, family** and a roofing uncle are his safety net, not unions.
He moves from **anxious** to panicked, with roofing as his escape in every scenario.
He wants **paid apprenticeships**, not handouts, and blames himself for lacking a trade.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, with only family to fall back on.
whatWouldHelp: Fast, **paid apprenticeships** to learn a trade.
**Money for learning**, not money for nothing.
